# Cardiac Amyloidosis: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and Epidemiology

Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is a progressive, infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by the extracellular deposition of misfolded protein as amyloid fibrils within the myocardium. Cardiac amyloidosis is caused by deposition of amyloid fibrils in the myocardium and has two main subtypes, transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis (ATTR) and immunoglobulin light chain cardiac amyloidosis (AL). [1] ATTR is further differentiated into wild-type (wtATTR) and hereditary (hATTR), depending on the absence or presence of mutation in the transthyretin gene. [1] Underlying these processes are well-characterized molecular mechanisms of protein misfolding and aggregation [2,3].

Once considered rare, CA is now recognized as relatively common. ATTRwt is an underdiagnosed disease that accounts for a significant number (13%) of HFpEF cases. [4] In addition, transthyretin amyloid has been identified in a meaningful proportion of patients with severe aortic stenosis undergoing transcatheter valve replacement [5]. International screening data confirm a high burden, with 56/315 (18%; 95% CI: 13.7–22.5) patients with evaluable scintigraphy having ATTR cardiomyopathy in a high-risk heart failure cohort [6]. Recent studies have suggested that up to 10% to 15% of older adults with HF may have unrecognized wtATTR. Associated features, including carpal tunnel syndrome and lumbar spinal stenosis, raise suspicion and may afford a means for early diagnosis. [7]

## Clinical Presentation and Diagnosis

CA should be suspected in patients with unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, and a constellation of extracardiac clues. Cardiac clues to diagnosis of amyloidosis includes increased left ventricular hypertrophy in the absence of hypertension or valvular heart disease, heart failure symptoms, diastolic dysfunction, atrial fibrillation, conduction system disease. [8] In AL amyloidosis, consideration of AL amyloidosis is crucial in patients with unexplained proteinuria, restrictive cardiomyopathy, peripheral neuropathy with autonomic features, bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, or hepatomegaly without imaging abnormalities. [9]

A transformative advance in diagnosis has been the validation of bone scintigraphy. Bone scintigraphy enables the diagnosis of cardiac ATTR amyloidosis to be made reliably without the need for histology in patients who do not have a monoclonal gammopathy. [10] Critically, the combined findings of grade 2 or 3 myocardial radiotracer uptake on bone scintigraphy and the absence of a monoclonal protein in serum or urine had a specificity and positive predictive value for cardiac ATTR amyloidosis of 100%. [10] Biomarkers, multimodality imaging, and expert consensus algorithms further support diagnosis and staging [11,12,13], with European and American consensus documents providing structured diagnostic frameworks [14,15]. The majority of cases (>98%) are related to monoclonal immunoglobulin light chain (AL) or transthyretin (ATTR) deposition. [14]

## Treatment of ATTR Cardiomyopathy

Therapeutic options have expanded dramatically. The landmark ATTR-ACT trial established TTR stabilization as effective: tafamidis binds to transthyretin, preventing tetramer dissociation and amyloidogenesis. In a multicenter, international, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial, we randomly assigned 441 patients with transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy in a 2:1:2 ratio to receive 80 mg of tafamidis, 20 mg of tafamidis, or placebo for 30 months. [16] Tafamidis reduced all-cause mortality and cardiovascular hospitalizations [16,17]. A newer stabilizer, acoramidis, has also demonstrated efficacy in phase 3 testing [18].

RNA-targeting therapies represent a second pillar. In APOLLO-B, administration of patisiran over a period of 12 months resulted in preserved functional capacity in patients with ATTR cardiac amyloidosis. [19] Subsequently, the HELIOS-B trial showed that vutrisiran was effective at preventing deaths and adverse events among patients with ATTR-CM. [20] Emerging strategies aim not merely to stabilize or silence TTR but to deplete existing deposits: in a phase 1 trial of the antibody NI006, at doses of at least 10 mg per kilogram, cardiac tracer uptake on scintigraphy and extracellular volume on cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, both of which are imaging-based surrogate markers of cardiac amyloid load, appeared to be reduced over a period of 12 months. [21] Gene editing offers a one-time approach; with NTLA-2001, administration of NTLA-2001 was associated with only mild adverse events and led to decreases in serum TTR protein concentrations through targeted knockout of TTR. [22]

## Treatment of AL Amyloidosis

AL amyloidosis is a plasma cell disorder requiring anti-clonal therapy. Systemic immunoglobulin light-chain (AL) amyloidosis is characterized by deposition of amyloid fibrils of light chains produced by clonal CD38+ plasma cells. Daratumumab, a human CD38-targeting antibody, may improve outcomes for this disease. [23] In the ANDROMEDA trial, adding daratumumab to bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone substantially increased hematologic complete response rates [23,24,25]. Management is guided by risk-adapted approaches and contemporary consensus [26,27,28], and overall multidisciplinary care—including supportive heart failure management, anticoagulation, and consideration of transplantation—remains essential [8,29,30].

## Conclusion

The recognition that the increased recognition of disease with the improvement in diagnostic armamentarium and serendipitous advancements in the therapeutic landscape have changed the status of CA from being a rare and untreatable disease to being a not-so-rare and treatable disease [1] encapsulates a remarkable decade of progress. Early diagnosis, enabled by noninvasive imaging and heightened clinical suspicion, is now paramount to maximize the benefit of an expanding therapeutic arsenal.
